content: The Union of South American Nations (UNASUR/UNASUL) is a developing supranational and intergovernmental organization that aims to integrate two existing free-trade blocs, Mercosur and the Andean Community, as part of a broader South American integration process. It is modeled after the European Union, with plans to establish a common currency, parliament, and passport system. The headquarters of the Union will be located in Quito, Ecuador, while the location of its financial institution, the Bank of the South, is still under discussion. The Union was previously known as the South American Community of Nations (CSN), but this designation was changed during the First South American Energy Summit on April 16, 2007. At the 10th meeting of the bloc's Foreign Ministers in Cartagena, Colombia, in January 2008, it was agreed that the UNASUR Treaty would be signed in June 2008 during the Third Summit of Heads of State. The foundation of the Union was announced at the Third South American Summit on December 8, 2004, when leaders from 12 South American nations signed the Cusco Declaration, a statement of intent to create the South American Community. Panama attended as an observer. The leaders expressed their intention to model the new community after the European Union, with a vision of achieving full integration by 2019, according to Allan Wagner, former Secretary General of the Andean Community. The operational framework of UNASUR was outlined during the First South American Community of Nations Heads of State Summit in Brasília on September 29-30, 2005. Initially, no new institutions will be created to avoid bureaucratic expansion, and existing institutions from the previous trade blocs will be utilized. A constitutional treaty is also expected to be drafted. The origins of this integration effort can be traced back to Simón Bolívar, who envisioned a federation of South American nations to ensure prosperity and security after independence. Although Bolívar's vision was not realized during his lifetime, UNASUR represents a concrete step toward achieving this goal. The provisional structure of UNASUR includes annual meetings of the presidents of member nations, biannual meetings of foreign ministers, and the establishment of a permanent secretariat in Quito, Ecuador. Former Ecuadorian President Rodrigo Borja has been nominated as Secretary General. Sectoral ministers' meetings will be convened as needed, and the presidency of the Union will rotate annually among member countries. UNASUR has initiated several projects, including the creation of a single market by eliminating tariffs on non-sensitive products by 2014 and sensitive products by 2019. Infrastructure cooperation is also a priority, with projects like the Interoceanic Highway, which aims to connect the Pacific Coast countries with Brazil and Argentina. The South American Energy Ring is another initiative to interconnect the region's energy resources, although political and economic challenges have delayed its implementation. The Union also promotes the free movement of people within South America, allowing citizens to travel visa-free for up to 90 days with just an identity card. On November 24, 2006, 12 South American countries waived visa requirements for tourism travel among their nationals. In terms of monetary policy, the South American Bank was officially launched in December 2007 in Buenos Aires, with a capital of $7 billion. Venezuela and Brazil are the primary contributors, and the bank's headquarters will be in Caracas, with offices in Buenos Aires and La Paz. The bank will finance development projects to enhance competitiveness and promote scientific and technological advancement in member countries. Defense policy is also a focus, with Venezuela and Brazil proposing the creation of a South American Defense Council to draft defense policies and strengthen regional security. UNASUR's full members include countries from the Andean Community (Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru) and Mercosur (Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, and Venezuela), along with Guyana, Suriname, and Chile. Observer states include Mexico and Panama. Non-participating territories include French Guiana, which is part of the European Union, and the Falkland Islands, South Georgia, and South Sandwich Islands, which are British overseas territories claimed by Argentina. The Union encompasses a population of 361 million people, covers an area of over 17 million square kilometers, and has a combined GDP of $2.65 trillion. It possesses 27% of the world's freshwater resources, 8 million square kilometers of forested land, and is a leading food producer and exporter. Most of its inhabitants share a single religion and speak either Portuguese or Spanish.
